title: Passive damping that removes resonant amplification from governing modes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a load-bearing structure whose members or ordinary connections dissipate enough vibration energy to keep resonant amplification small across the modes that govern strength and occupant acceleration. Damping would be built into the primary structural system, operate passively without external power, and require no auxiliary tuned mass. The objective is a useful system-level response across several governing modes, rather than a favorable material property or suppression of one selected frequency.

Existing vibration-control approaches provide important precedents. Tuned-mass dampers use a secondary moving mass as an energy sink, while viscous, frictional and viscoelastic systems provide other forms of passive dissipation. Supplemental damping is therefore not universally tied to a single tuned frequency. The proposed advance would need to demonstrate a particular combination: dissipation integrated into primary members or ordinary joints, effective control of multiple governing modes, and robustness to changes in structural properties.

Interpretation of the target: removing resonant amplification means reducing its design significance within a defined operating envelope. It need not mean eliminating every local response peak, achieving critical damping, or preventing every possible form of vibration. The candidate's suggested dynamic-magnification limit of about 2 is a proposed operational target whose meaning depends on the excitation, response quantity and normalization.

significance.text: Low inherent damping makes resonance an important concern in dynamically sensitive buildings and bridges. The June 2024 STRUCTURE practice article reports typical U.S. wind-serviceability damping assumptions of about 1–2% of critical damping and typical seismic-analysis assumptions of about 5%. It also describes cases in which measured tall-building damping is substantially below design assumptions. Reliable engineered dissipation could reduce the uncertainty and design penalties associated with relying on small, variable inherent damping.

Conditional consequence: if primary members or ordinary joints could maintain low amplification across all governing modes while retaining adequate strength, stiffness, stability and durability, the direct benefit would be reduced resonant motion within the demonstrated conditions. Integrating that capability into the load-bearing system could also reduce dependence on auxiliary tuned masses and their associated space and mass requirements. This would be a substantial change for structures whose serviceability or strength is controlled by resonant response.

Lighter towers or decks, more usable floor area, and greater heights or spans are possible downstream benefits where dynamic response currently drives stiffness or material requirements. The practice article explains that increasing tower stiffness can add material cost and reduce usable space. Such savings would nevertheless require project-specific redesign and verification; they do not follow automatically from a damping improvement.

Engineering limits on that inference: damping does not remove static gravity loads, buckling, drift limits, fatigue, aerodynamic instability or other constraints on buildings and bridges. Lower resonant amplification also does not guarantee an undamaged structure during an earthquake or eliminate transient response. The revolutionary claim is therefore conditional on a demanding combination of structural performance and reliable dissipation, rather than an expectation that damping alone makes height, span or safety unrestricted.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is primary-structure passive dissipation strong and reliable enough to keep amplification below a specified limit across the modes governing both strength and acceleration. The supplied sources motivate that target through low inherent damping and established vibration-control needs. They do not establish that this exact combination remains unachieved worldwide as of November 1, 2026, so its present-day absence remains an open evidence question.

Engineering synthesis: a central barrier is obtaining substantial energy dissipation without sacrificing the stiffness, strength and stability required of the same load-bearing members and connections. Performance must persist over the relevant frequency range and at the excitation amplitudes that matter for wind serviceability and seismic response. A mechanism effective under one loading condition cannot simply be assumed to remain effective under another.

Engineering synthesis: system integration is another barrier. Dissipation must engage through the deformation patterns of several governing modes, including modes that may produce little motion at a particular joint or measurement location. The structure must also retain useful performance when mass, stiffness, loading or environmental conditions change. Bandwidth and resistance to detuning are already recognized evaluation dimensions in the 2026 review, but its supplied abstract does not demonstrate the proposed primary-structure solution.

Engineering synthesis: scaling from a material or connection to a complete structure requires showing that repeated energy dissipation remains compatible with durability and ordinary structural use. A high material loss modulus alone would not establish modal damping or acceptable building response. The earlier assertion that laboratory composites already provide the relevant coupon results is not documented by the supplied evidence and cannot serve as an established step toward this capability.

current_state.text: Ron Aquino, Shayne Love and Jamieson Robinson's June 13, 2024 STRUCTURE article, “Discussing Engineered Damping,” reports that ASCE 7-22 commentary values of about 1–2% damping are typically used for U.S. wind serviceability and about 5% is typically used for each mode in seismic analysis. These are reported analysis assumptions, not universal measured properties. The article also reports completed-building measurements below half the damping assumed during design for common wind events. The supplied review had the substantive article text; ASCE 7-22 itself was not supplied, so the code-commentary attribution remains mediated through the practice article.

The November 6, 2022 Sensors article, “Review of Vibration Control Strategies of High-Rise Buildings,” reports natural damping in flexible structures ranging from 0.1% to 5%. It describes tuned-mass dampers as secondary-mass energy sinks and surveys broader passive and active control strategies, including passive viscous systems. These are review findings about a range of structures and technologies, rather than new full-scale measurements establishing one common damping value. The supplied review used retained full-text XML containing the article and tables; figure images were not supplied or inspected.

The March 21, 2026 review by Saifullah Arabzai, Mehtab Ahmad, Md Sajid and Kong Fah Tee, “Advanced damping devices for tall buildings under seismic and wind loads: A state-of-the-art review,” reports in its abstract that reviewed literature generally finds acceleration and displacement reductions of 40–60% for well-tuned passive systems. The range depends on hazard type, tuning strategy and structural configuration. Its abstract also states that multiple tuned-mass dampers and inerter-based variants broaden control bandwidth and improve detuning robustness with smaller physical masses. These are reported reductions from reviewed control systems, not evidence that primary structural resonance has disappeared across governing modes.

Only the 2026 article's subscription preview and abstract were available in the supplied review. Its underlying studies, comparison methods and full technical qualifications were therefore not inspected. The numerical range can be retained as an attributed abstract-level report, but cannot be treated as independently verified performance for every passive system or directly converted into the proposed dynamic-magnification threshold.

Evidence boundary: the supplied record establishes low inherent damping, examples of unexpectedly low measured damping, and established supplemental vibration-control approaches. It supplies no demonstrated structure meeting the full STR-11 proposal. Because the bounded freshness-search record is empty, that lack of a supplied demonstration does not establish that no qualifying result exists as of November 1, 2026. The innovation remains a hypothetical target in this record, with current worldwide achievement unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: test a multi-story frame or flexible deck large enough to have several governing modes within a specified wind or seismic frequency band. Dissipation must come from its primary load-bearing members and ordinary connections, without an auxiliary tuned mass or external power. Define the governing modes and the structural integration boundary before testing. A single-mode tuned-mass demonstration or a high-loss-modulus coupon would not establish this system capability.
completion_criteria.label: Primary structural damping demonstrated passively across several governing modes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed response criterion: predefine the excitation, measured response quantities, amplitude range and dynamic-magnification normalization, then require magnification below about 2 throughout each governing modal frequency region. Base-motion input and wind-force input require different transfer-function definitions and must not be compared as if their ratios were interchangeable. Search across each modal region to capture shifted peaks, and use enough response locations to avoid mistaking a measurement point near a mode's node for suppression of that mode. The numerical threshold is a proposal, not an established consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Magnification below about 2 throughout each governing modal region

completion_criteria.text: Proposed robustness challenge: repeat the measurements after a specified mass change large enough to materially detune a comparable single-mode tuned-mass damper, and require the same response limit. Report the associated changes in modal frequencies and shapes. This challenge would test whether the result depends narrowly on the original configuration; it would not establish robustness to every possible modification.
completion_criteria.label: Response limit maintained after a materially detuning mass change

completion_criteria.text: Proposed structural and reproducibility requirements: document acceptable strength, stiffness and stability alongside vibration suppression, and repeat the demonstration over declared loading amplitudes, environmental conditions and dissipation cycles relevant to the intended use. Provide the structural configuration, connection details, excitation records, measurements and analysis definitions needed for independent reproduction. Durability claims should match the tested exposure and cycling history.
completion_criteria.label: Structural adequacy and repeatable suppression documented for independent reproduction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary: successful finite tests would establish performance for the tested structures, modes and conditions. Claims about other building forms, bridge decks, hazards or service lives would require further evidence. Acceptance should distinguish reduced resonant amplification from complete absence of peaks, critical damping, damage prevention and universal vibration control.
completion_criteria.label: Performance claims confined to tested structures, modes and conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison with STR-05, “Primary members whose mechanical state can be reprogrammed in service”: both place unusual mechanical capability in the primary structure. STR-11 concerns always-on passive dissipation without external power; STR-05's title concerns changing a member's mechanical state during service. Those capabilities could coexist, but neither implies the other. Only STR-05's title is supplied, so its detailed mechanisms and overlap cannot be verified here.

Roster-based comparison with STR-04, “Field-scale broadband seismic cloaking,” and STR-10, “Ordinary buildings that remain undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes”: all concern structural response to dynamic loading. STR-11 targets energy dissipation and resonant amplification within the structure. STR-04 identifies a seismic-cloaking objective, while STR-10 identifies an earthquake damage and usability outcome. Meeting STR-11's response criterion would not by itself demonstrate either cloaking or post-earthquake usability.

Roster-based comparison with STR-01, “Flaw-tolerant bulk members at near-theoretical specific strength,” STR-03, “A cast mineral solid that can be a complete primary structure,” and STR-08, “Primary structure that stores the host system’s useful energy”: these entries share an emphasis on capabilities embedded in load-bearing material or members. Their stated targets concern strength, a complete structural material system, and useful energy storage, respectively. Dissipating vibration energy does not establish near-theoretical strength, material completeness or recoverable energy storage.

Roster-based comparison with STR-02, “Repeated autonomous restoration of full structural capacity,” STR-06, “Load-bearing structures that grow and remodel,” and STR-09, “A prospectively validated law of structural lifespan”: these address restoration, adaptation or prediction over time. STR-11 addresses dynamic response during loading. Effective damping could be relevant to lifetime demands, but would not demonstrate autonomous repair, growth or a validated lifespan law.

Roster-based comparison with STR-07, “Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism,” and STR-12, “Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member”: these concern collapse mechanisms and structural robustness. Reduced resonant demand may complement those objectives, but does not establish that an undesigned mechanism is unavailable or that loss of any primary member cannot trigger disproportionate collapse. These remain separate capabilities.

unresolved_issues: Whether any structure already meets the combined integration, multimode suppression and robustness target as of November 1, 2026 remains unresolved because the supplied freshness-search record is empty.
The physical mechanism and structural implementation that could deliver the proposed performance while retaining strength, stiffness, stability and durability are unspecified.
The proposed magnification limit of about 2 still requires application-specific normalization, input and output definitions, frequency bands, amplitude ranges and governing-mode selection.
The magnitude of the mass-change challenge and the comparable tuned-mass reference system remain to be specified.
The underlying comparisons supporting the 2026 review's reported 40–60% reductions remain uninspected because only its preview and abstract were supplied.
The ASCE 7-22 commentary values are supported through the 2024 practice article; the original commentary was not supplied.
No supplied source establishes the earlier laboratory-composite loss-modulus assertion.
Detailed comparisons with the other roster entries, particularly STR-05, remain limited by the absence of their full concept records.

brief.title: Buildings and bridges that absorb their own shaking
possible: People could use buildings and bridges whose beams, columns and ordinary joints absorb enough vibration energy to keep repeated pushes from building into large motions. The load-bearing structure would do this without external power or an extra moving weight.

The protection would cover several modes—the different patterns in which a structure vibrates—that matter for strength and occupant comfort. It would keep working when changes in the structure shift those patterns.
why: For occupants, less shaking would mean greater comfort. For engineers, reliable energy absorption would reduce dependence on small, uncertain amounts of natural damping, the process that dissipates vibration energy.

Integrating this function into the structure could free space otherwise occupied by moving weights used to control vibration. Where shaking drives design, it could also open the way to lighter structures, more usable floor area or longer spans.

sources.who: Ron Aquino, Shayne Love and Jamieson Robinson
sources.showed: They report that some completed buildings dissipate much less vibration energy than designers assumed. They also describe established systems for reducing building motion.
sources.quote: Motioneering, Inc. has measured inherent damping of completed buildings that is less than half of what was assumed during design for common wind events.
sources.cited_for: Uncertain natural damping affects building motion, design costs and usable space.
sources.not_established: The article does not demonstrate ordinary load-bearing members or joints controlling all governing modes without an extra moving mass.

sources.who: Mohamed Hechmi El Ouni, Mahdi Abdeddaim, Said Elias and Nabil Ben Kahla
sources.showed: Their review describes vibration-control systems already used in tall buildings, including devices that absorb energy without external power.
sources.quote: Most of them have already been practically used in real-life high-rise buildings.
sources.cited_for: Passive vibration control is established, with several approaches beyond an extra moving weight.
sources.not_established: The review does not establish the combined target of structural integration, control across governing modes and robustness to mass changes.

sources.who: Saifullah Arabzai, Mehtab Ahmad, Md Sajid and Kong Fah Tee
sources.showed: Their review reports reduced building motion from passive devices. It also describes arrangements that control a wider range of vibration frequencies and better tolerate changes in structural properties.
sources.quote: Viscous dampers excel under short-duration, high-velocity seismic demands, whereas viscoelastic devices perform more effectively for long-duration wind-induced serviceability, with hybrid systems leveraging the advantages of both.
sources.cited_for: Existing devices reduce motion, and their performance depends on loading and structural configuration.
sources.not_established: Reported motion reductions do not demonstrate the proposed response limit across governing modes using primary members or ordinary joints.

shown: Engineers already use passive devices to reduce motion in tall buildings. Reviews describe systems using moving weights, liquids and other energy-absorbing devices, including arrangements that work across a wider range of vibration frequencies.

Aquino and colleagues report measurements showing why better control matters: some buildings have much less natural damping than assumed. These results do not establish the full combination of load-bearing integration, control across governing modes and resistance to structural changes.
missing: A structural mechanism must absorb substantial vibration energy while preserving strength, stiffness and stability.
A whole structure must limit amplification across the vibration patterns governing both strength and occupant acceleration.
The same response limit must survive a meaningful mass change and repeated use under relevant loading and environmental conditions.

milestones.label: Load-bearing parts suppress several governing vibration patterns
milestones.explanation: A frame or deck would have to dissipate energy through primary members and ordinary joints across several governing modes, without power or an extra tuned weight. This would establish control at the scale of a structure.

milestones.label: Amplification stays below about twice the defined reference response
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to keep the response ratio below about 2 throughout each governing mode's frequency range, using predefined inputs, amplitudes, reference responses and measurement locations. This would establish a clear performance limit.

milestones.label: The response limit survives a substantial mass change
milestones.explanation: The structure would have to meet the same limit after a mass change large enough to disrupt a comparable tuned moving-weight device. This would test whether control depends narrowly on the original configuration.

milestones.label: Structural performance and repeatable suppression support independent reproduction
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish structural adequacy and repeatable suppression across declared loads, environments and use cycles, with enough detail for independent reproduction. This would connect vibration control to structural use.

milestones.label: Claims stay within tested structures, modes and conditions
milestones.explanation: Claims would have to match the structures, modes and conditions tested. This would distinguish reduced amplification from eliminating all vibration peaks, preventing damage or controlling every kind of motion.

uncertain: Whether any structure already meets the complete combination of requirements remains unresolved.
The proposed amplification limit needs precise definitions of the loading, measured response, reference response and governing modes.
The size of the mass change and the comparable moving-weight system used to judge robustness remain unspecified.

page.title: Multimode passive direct damping of buildings
page.definition: A building’s load-bearing members or connections dissipate vibration energy without external power or a separately tuned moving weight. The system meets wind and earthquake response limits across the vibration patterns, called modes, governing strength and occupant acceleration, throughout its declared range of mass and stiffness.

goal.need: Motioneering reports completed-building damping below half the design assumption during common wind events; the sample size is not stated. Aquino and colleagues illustrate approximately ±20% changes in calculated acceleration and wind-induced drift associated with a 30% coefficient of variation in damping. This uncertainty affects the damping contribution that designers can credit.

figures.caption: Damping assumptions reported by Aquino and colleagues.
figures.note: These are reported analysis assumptions, not universal measured properties. Critical damping is the boundary between oscillatory and nonoscillatory free response.

statements.body: ASCE/SEI Task Committee for the Design and Performance of Tall Buildings for Wind
statements.quote: appropriate supplemental damping technology for strength design of the primary structural system.
statements.context: Section 7.5 identifies extending supplemental damping from wind serviceability to structural strength design as an industry objective.

statements.quote: to increase the level of inherent damping of tall coupled shear wall buildings to control wind-induced and earthquake-induced dynamic vibrations
statements.context: The developers state the purpose of viscoelastic coupling dampers, which replace coupling beams connecting structural walls.

completion.title: A building meets its response limits with passive direct damping throughout its declared property range.
completion.criterion: An independently reviewed full-scale demonstration, supported by component tests and validated response analysis, establishes that passive damping in primary members or connections keeps strength demands, drift and occupant acceleration within externally specified project limits in every governing mode, throughout the declared mass, stiffness, loading-amplitude and temperature ranges. The control requires neither external operating power nor an auxiliary tuned mass. Project authorities must specify numerical response limits and property ranges before assessment.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body’s published test covering the complete combination was identified.
completion.basis: ASCE 7-22 Chapter 18, ASCE MOP 143, and VCD design, prototype and field reports were searched for a joint test of primary-structure integration, governing-mode suppression and mass/stiffness variation. None was found. This fallback uses externally specified project response limits; it does not adopt the draft’s amplification factor of 2. Achievement of the complete test is not established.

milestones.title: Two full-size structural dampers withstand at least 2,000 reversed wind cycles without damage.
milestones.criterion: Test two full-size devices per type and size for the design windstorm’s cycle count, at least 2,000, at design amplitudes and frequency 1/T1; T1 is the fundamental period. Apply representative gravity loading and thermal conditions and meet the no-damage criterion. Approved representative sizes and alternative protocols are permitted. Pant and colleagues tested one full-size coupling damper under six-hour wind histories; that result does not establish complete ASCE qualification.
milestones.threshold_quote: 2,000 continuous fully reversed cycles of wind load.

milestones.title: Structural dampers pass the 10-, 5- and 3-cycle seismic prototype tests.
milestones.criterion: At ambient temperature and frequency 1/(1.5T1), pass 10, 5 and 3 reversed cycles at 0.33, 0.67 and 1.0 times the risk-targeted maximum-considered-earthquake device displacement. Meet Section 18.6.2.5 force, stiffness and hysteresis-loop-energy criteria, generally using 15% tolerances, and required temperature/frequency tests. Larger tolerances require design justification. Pant and colleagues also tested their specimen using project earthquake histories; those tests do not establish complete qualification.

milestones.title: A damped building design meets wind limits and seismic strength and drift acceptance criteria.
milestones.criterion: Meet Chapter 18 strength requirements and maximum earthquake drift ≤3% of story height and ≤the Table 12.12-1 limit multiplied by min(1.5R/Cd, 1.9); R and Cd are the code’s structural-system coefficients. Meet project wind strength, drift and acceleration limits under MOP 143. A 2023 numerical study of 47-, 57- and 65-story Vancouver buildings found wind-serviceability compliance with coupling dampers; that result alone does not establish complete acceptance.
milestones.set_by: ASCE/SEI 7-22, Section 18.4; ASCE/SEI task committee, MOP 143, Chapters 2–3.
milestones.threshold_quote: The maximum drift at MCER shall neither exceed 3%

milestones.title: Field measurements confirm a completed building’s specified wind-response performance.
milestones.criterion: Field measurements confirm the completed building’s specified damping and occupant-motion performance for its governing wind modes, following MOP 143 Section 10.3.1. Partial evidence appears in a 2020 developer report: one 66-story Toronto building had 42 coupling dampers on 21 levels and a target of 0.9 percentage points of added fundamental-mode damping, reportedly exceeded during a wind event assigned a five-year return period. This report is not peer reviewed and does not establish performance in every governing mode.
milestones.set_by: ASCE/SEI task committee, MOP 143, Section 10.3.1, recommended field validation; the numerical example is the published YC Condominiums project target.
milestones.threshold_quote: to ensure that the building is performing as expected

not_found: No outside test defining removal of resonant amplification, an amplification limit of 2, or a prescribed mass-change challenge was found.
No opened result established the complete governing-mode response test throughout a specified mass-and-stiffness range.
The publisher and SSRN pages for the 2025 paper “Full-scale monitoring of a tall, slender building with viscoelastic coupling dampers” could not be opened.

results.finding: Two full-size viscoelastic damping units were cycled 10,000 times at a 10-mil equivalent amplitude.
results.detail: The text does not establish that the units were undamaged after cycling or that the amplitude represented design wind conditions. Representative gravity loading and the full thermal conditions are not established.
results.quote:
Two tests were run with an equivalent amplitude of
10 mils for 10,000 cycles, and two tests were run with an equivalent
amplitude of 19 mils until fatigue was noticed.

results.finding: DMAX dampers: 20 prototypes were tested in a program that included 2,000 wind-loading cycles.
results.detail: The guide reports consistent dynamic performance, but does not specify how many prototypes underwent wind loading or establish no damage, representative gravity loading, design amplitudes, or frequency 1/T1.
results.quote:
Wind loading phase
•    2000 cycles at 70% of the specified slip resistance

results.finding: Twenty DMAX prototypes showed dynamic performance with a reported tolerance below ±15%.
results.detail: The Lehigh program included cyclic and wind loading, but the guide does not establish all Section 18.6.2.5 force, stiffness and hysteresis-loop-energy criteria or the required temperature and frequency tests. It describes HCAI qualification as in progress.
results.quote: Unique dynamic performance with a tolerance lower than +/-15% tested at Lehigh Structures lab, US

results.finding: Two 60-story towers: predicted 10-year wind acceleration was 9.4 milli-g with damping.
results.detail: The prediction is below the stated 15 milli-g residential comfort limit. The paper does not establish the specified Chapter 18 strength, maximum earthquake drift, or MOP 143 wind criteria. The project design was peer reviewed, but the text does not establish that the conference paper was peer reviewed.

results.finding: One hospital design, analyzed with 10 earthquake records, had maximum considered earthquake interstory drift below 2%.
results.detail: The design used viscous wall dampers and met stated seismic performance goals, but the text does not establish all specified Chapter 18 strength and drift limits or project wind strength, drift and acceleration limits under MOP 143.
